title: Reporting Injuries: OSHA Recordkeeping
summary: OSHA recordkeeping has three parts: recording work-related injuries and illnesses, reporting severe ones to OSHA, and annual electronic submission of data. Records help find and remove hazards.
talking_points: Recording and reporting help employers, workers, and OSHA find and eliminate hazards and prevent future injuries and illnesses.
Many employers with more than 10 employees must record work-related injuries and illnesses on OSHA forms 300, 300A, and 301, or equivalent forms. Certain industries are exempt.
All employers must notify OSHA within 8 hours of a work-related death.
All employers must notify OSHA within 24 hours of a work-related in-patient hospitalization, amputation, or loss of an eye.
Some establishments must submit injury and illness data electronically once per year, from January 2 to March 2, through OSHA's Injury Tracking Application.
Good practice, not an OSHA requirement: report every injury to your supervisor so it can be recorded and reported correctly.
site_hazards_to_check: Injuries not reported to a supervisor
No one assigned to keep the injury and illness forms up to date
Unclear who reports a severe injury to OSHA and how fast
Reporting deadlines unknown to the crew supervisors
discussion_questions: Who on our team keeps the injury and illness records?
What are the two OSHA reporting deadlines, and what triggers each?
Why does it help us to report even minor injuries?
